How to plan content for a business website

A useful content plan begins with what customers need to understand, not a target number of articles. The best first project may be rewriting a service page, improving product information, or combining several overlapping guides.

By Shahir Salehi3 minute readPractical guide

In this guide

  1. Collect the real questions
  2. Give each page a job
  3. Audit before expanding
  4. Write briefs that support good work
  5. Connect the pages
  6. Choose a sustainable cadence
  7. Evaluate purpose, not volume

Collect the real questions

Review customer conversations, inquiries, sales objections, support requests, and existing search data where available. Separate questions asked before choosing a provider from questions asked after purchase. For a consulting service, a buyer may need to understand scope and access requirements; for a product, they may need sizing or compatibility. Those needs should determine the information you publish.

Give each page a job

Define the audience, primary question, page type, and next step. A service page should explain an offering; an article can help someone understand a problem; a resource can support a specific task. If two proposed pages have the same purpose and answer the same question, one stronger page may be more useful than two slightly different keyword versions.

Audit before expanding

List existing pages and assess accuracy, usefulness, duplication, and ownership. Record whether to keep, improve, combine, or retire each one. A page with little traffic may still answer an important contractual or customer question. If removing a page, consider incoming links and a relevant replacement. Do not redirect every retired URL to the homepage simply to avoid an error code.

Write briefs that support good work

A brief should include the intended reader, important questions, verified facts, sources requiring review, a proposed structure, related links, and the intended action. It should also identify who approves business claims. This is especially important when using outside writers or AI assistance: a fluent draft can still contain invented details that sound convincing.

Connect the pages

Create links where they help a reader continue. A technical guide can link to a relevant service and to a deeper explanation of one step. A services hub should make specialist pages discoverable. Descriptive anchors are more useful than repeated read more links with no context. Avoid adding a large list of keyword links to every article.

Choose a sustainable cadence

Research, review, editing, publishing, and maintenance all take time. A small business may be better served by a limited set of well-maintained pages than a weekly publishing target it cannot support. Assign an owner and a review trigger for time-sensitive content. Record actual publication and revision dates; do not invent a history to make the site look established.

Evaluate purpose, not volume

Review whether pages answer useful questions, attract relevant visitors, and support qualified inquiries or customer understanding. Not every article needs an immediate lead. Combine quantitative evidence with customer feedback and the editorial assessment of whether information remains accurate. Use the findings to improve the library before expanding it.

Put it into practice

  • Start with customer questions and existing evidence.
  • Assign a distinct purpose to every page.
  • Audit and consolidate before adding more.
  • Require factual approval and useful internal links.
  • Budget time for maintenance as well as publication.
